ABSTRACT: Rapid discovery of a deep eutectic solvent (DES) and its increasing application in various scientific applications demands a well-defined polarity scale for the new generation of eutectic solvents. The tunable nature of a DES facilitates to increase its number by combining various hydrogen bond acceptors and donors in multiple molar ratios. In this context, we have developed a first-principle-based conductor-like screening model-real solvent (COSMO-RS)-derived predictive modeling approach to predict the Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters of 26 hydrophilic and 62 hydrophobic DESs. The COSMO-RS-derived energies, that is, hydrogen bonding energy (EHB), misfit energy (EMF), and van der Waals energy (EVDW), are linearly correlated with the experimental data set of 28 DESs having 4 choline chloride, 17 tetraalkylammonium organic salt, 4 menthol, and 3 betaine subclasses. A lowest root-mean-square deviation (rmsd) of 0.06% for the choline chloride class of DESs and a highest rmsd of 3.14% for the tetrabutylammonium chloride class of DESs are obtained. Therefore, the correlated models are then extended to develop 60 DESs consisting of 15 choline chloride DESS, 4 different hydrophilic DESs, 17 tetraalkylammonium organic salt origin DESs, 7 menthol DESs, and 17 thymol-based DESs.

# 1. INTRODUCTION A deep eutectic solvent (DES) is rapidly emerging as a new kind of green solvent prepared from low-cost abundant resources. It is prepared by a mixture of organic salt and hydrogen bond donor (HBD) in a definitive molar ratio with the melting point lower than that of the individual components. Therefore, the formation of a stable DES depends on the strength of the HBD and hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA). Often, the organic salt contains a cation and an anion, where the cation acts as an additional HBD. However, a natural compound such as menthol or thymol can form a DES with carboxylic acid. Here, menthol or thymol acts as a HBA and carboxylic acid acts as a HBD. By varying the molar ratio of the components, combining different organic salts with HBD, or mixing natural compounds and carboxylic acids, a large number of DESs has been proposed in the literature. 1,2 Therefore, the physiochemical properties of DESs can be tuned depending on the molar compositions of the respective components.3 The tunable properties open up the feasibility of application of DES as a solvent in phase equilibria, 4 catalysis, 5 and chemical synthesis. 6 The combination of HBA and HBD gives DES the ability to accept and donate protons during solvation and thus form a hydrogen bond with the solute. This enhances the dissolution capability of DES, due to which it is widely used as a solvent in separation and purification processes. 7,8
One of the important properties of a solvent is polarity. Polarity defines the possible interactions between a solute and a solvent. Additionally, the polarity of a solvent influences the

reaction rate, mechanism, solvation ability, and product yield. ^9 The experimental measurement of polarity involves the analysis of shifting UV–vis absorbance spectra of solvatochro- mic probes. A simplistic polarity scale is a one-parameter Dimroth–Reichardt E_T(30) scale which can only provide qualitative trends. ^10 The hydrogen bond donating ability of a solvent influences the E_T(30) polarity scale, which merely measures the polarizability. Kamlet and Taft^11 have developed a multiparametric model using a set of solvatochromic probes to assess the ability of HBD (acidity) and HBA (basicity) and polarizability of the same solvent. However, all the dyes are expensive. Further, the selection of dye and experimental approach influence the solvatochromic parame- ters. 12 Therefore, the continuous improvement of experimental data set coupled with the expensive experiment makes it harder to follow a definitive chart of polarity scale.

As a state-of-the-art green solvent and its ever-growing application in the separation and purification processes, construction of polarity chart becomes utmost necessity. However, a handful of literature studies are available regarding the experimental measurement of K–T parameters of DESs. Six ChCl-based DESs, four menthol-based DESs, and three quaternary ammonium-based DESs are reported by Florindo et al.13 The K–T parameters of 13 ChCl-based DESs and 3 betaine-based DESs are being reported by Cai et al.14 Teles et al. further reported the α and β values of 19 quaternary ammonium salt-based DESs.15 The K–T parameters of two quaternary ammonium salt-based DESs and one betaine-based DES are reported by Dietz et al.16 However, like other solvents, the reported data of solvatochromic parameters may vary upon the change of dye.15 The HBD and HBA present in the DES make distinctive interactions with the solute. Further, the inherent H-bond interaction between the HBA and HBD increases the complexity of nonbonded interactions with the solute. Because of the large number of DES, it will be an expensive endeavor for the experimental measurement of solvatochromic parameters of every DES. Therefore, a priori modeling of solvatochromic parameters and construction of polarity scale would ensure benchmark database for the future applications of DESs. However, to date, there is no modeling approach for the solvatochromic parameters of DESs. Hence, a modeling technique with a similar class of compounds having analogous physiochemical behavior and applications would create a benchmark step for future development.

The combinatorial nature of construction, tunable nature in physiochemical properties, and their similar applications bring DESs in close analogy with ionic liquids (ILs). Therefore, to construct a predictive polarity chart of DES, we can highlight some of the modeling approaches of the solvatochromic parameters reported for ILs. To establish a well-defined, consistent, and predictive approach of solvatochromic parameters, several modeling approaches have been attempted in the literature for the case of ILs. Mente and Maroncelli performed the Monte Carlo (MC) simulation of solvent interactions in the E_T(30) scale of solvent polarity. 17 Znamenskiy and Kobrak explored the polarity of ILs using a solvatochromic dye by molecular dynamics (MD) simula- tion. 18 However, both the methods are computationally expensive. Contreras et al. proposed an empirical energy density model based on the Lewis molecular acidity of ILs. 19 Niedermeyer et al. proposed time-dependent density func- tional theory (TD-DFT) calculation involving the interaction between solvents and K-T dyes for the prediction of K-T parameters. 20 Recently, Cláudio et al. 21 and Kurnia et al. 22 predicted β and α values using the quantum chemical (QC)- based conductor-like screening model-real solvent (COSMO- RS) approach. The unimolecular QC calculation of cation and anion and subsequent correlation with the β and α values shall
open up a computationally inexpensive rapid screening of solvents.

In this context, we have developed a QC-based predictive approach for the hydrogen bond (H-bond) acidity (α) and hydrogen bond basicity (β) of DESs. First-principle-based predictive model COSMO-RS has been used to predict the various nonbonded interactions of DESs. The predicted nonbonded interactions are then correlated with the experimentally measured values of α and β. The correlation coefficients are later employed to develop an extended scale of predictive models.

## 2. COMPUTATIONAL METHOD ### 2.1. COSMO-RS Theory. COSMO-RS is a QC-based predictive model, where various thermodynamic properties are calculated depending on the structure of molecules. Here, molecules are assumed to be submerged in an ideal virtual conductor environment. The interactions are thereby calculated at the interface of the molecules and conductor, considering the counter-polarization and electrostatic screening. Thereafter, the molecules are considered as a collection of surface segments, and the screening charge of each segment is computed. The screening charge density, position, and area of each segment of the surface are stored in a file named "COSMO" file (.cosmo extension). Later, the pairwise interactions between the two segments are computed with a set of statistical mechanical calculations given in the literature.23,24 Misfit energy originates from the nonideal contact of two segments. van der Waals' energy is a summation of dispersion energy and cavity formation energy. The cavity formation energy arises because of the formation of a cavity inside the conductor medium to accept a molecule from the gas phase to the conductor medium. The inhomogeneous charges on the molecular surface are adequately represented by the dispersion energy. Hydrogen bond (H-bond) plays a crucial role in the formation of DES. Therefore, we have used the modified version of COSMO-RS to adequately represent the H-bond interaction in the predictive modeling.25

The screening charge densities of surface segments are standardized to accommodate into equally spaced 71 discrete bins from -0.035 to +0.035 e/Å² (an increment of 0.001 e/ Å²). Therefore, a normalized histogram of segmental areas is plotted within the limits of bins, better known as sigma profile (σ-profile). The σ-profile is the characteristic distribution of charge densities and is unique for every molecule. However, modified COSMO-RS theory segregates the hydrogen bonding segments using a Gaussian-type probability in the original σ- profile. The same is not added with the nonhydrogen bonding segmental areas. The segregation results in the representation of two σ-profiles, that is, the hydrogen bonding σ-profile and the nonhydrogen bonding σ-profile. Considering the possible attraction among the atomic pairs, the dispersion energy term is calculated by the first-order mean field term. Further, the cavity formation energy is calculated from the thermodynamics perturbation theory. The description of each energetic term and the corresponding COSMO parameters are adapted from the literature. 25,26

## 3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION The COSMO-RS-based predictive modeling has been used on 88 types of DESs, of which 26 are of hydrophilic class and the rest belong to the hydrophobic class of DESs. The hydrophilic class is further subdivided into 19 choline chloride (ChCl)-based DESs, 3 other choline cation-based DESs, 3 betaine class of DESs, and 1 ethyl(2-hydroxyethyl) dimethylammonium class of DES. The hydrophobic class is further subdivided to 34 tetraalkylammonium salt-based DESs (including chloride and bromide anions), 11 menthol-based DESs, and 17 thymol-based DESs. The complete number of DESs along with the model prediction and the extended scale of the predicted K–T parameters are given in Table S1 of the Supporting Information. Further, the structure of HBAs and HBDs and their respective energies E_HB, E_MF, and E_VDW are given in Tables S2–S6 of the Supporting Information.

The α parameter describes the capacity of a solvent to donate protons in solvent to solute H-bonding, whereas the β parameter describes the ability of accepting a proton.15 The predictive models (M1α-M8α and M1β-M8β) are hereby used to predict 19 types of hydrophilic and 41 types of hydrophobic DESs. ## 3.5. Suitable Methodologies of Prediction of K–T Parameters and Future Scope of Development. In the previous section, predictive approaches such as MD–MC simulation, QC calculations, and COSMO-RS framework are discussed with respect to the possible modeling pathways of K–T parameters. In the MD and MC approaches, the K–T parameters were predicted with respect to the interactions with the solvatochromic dye. However, force fields of ILs as well as DES are not reliably developed. Therefore, the accuracy of the predicted data set always remains questionable when adopting the MD approach. However, both the approaches are computationally expensive, and considering the ever-growing number of DES, the construction of such database with these approaches will take a long time. Therefore, these approaches are not suitable for a priori prediction. On the other hand, the QC-based calculation of the DES–dye complex will be

relatively faster. However, generalized models based on the electronic structure calculation will likely accumulate large error in the database. This work is also derived from the optimized geometry from the electronic structure calculation coupled with the COSMO-RS formulation. In order to reduce the large error, it has been observed from the derived data set that an individual model based on the subclasses of DES shall improve the accuracy. However, the accuracy of our prediction mainly depends on the accurate theoretical description with respect to various interaction energies in the COSMO-RS framework. Therefore, the predicted and extended scale of database can be further improved by incorporating various interaction parameters given in the literature. 35,36 The existing experimental methodology of K–T parameters involves extensive solvatochromic probe. For an ever-growing list of DES, the continuous experimentation poses serious economic challenge. Further, the experimental polarity scale depends on the set of solvatochromic dyes as well as purity of the DES. Hence, the present methodology emphasizes on the identi- fication of subclasses of DES, followed by the creation of experimental data set of small number of DES of that subclass. Next, the predictive models developed within the framework of this work can predict the extended scale of K–T parameters of other DESs in the same subclass. However, a futuristic development could be the generalized model based on the group interaction parameter. However, this depends on the accurate description of interaction energies. Based on the accurate description of interaction energies of functional moieties of DES, the interaction parameters can be listed and from that the list of generalized model can be formulated.

## 4. CONCLUSIONS COSMO-RS-predicted hydrogen bonding, misfit, and van der Waals energies were calculated and correlated in a four- parameter model to predict the Kamlet-Taft H-bond acidity and H-bond basicity of DESs. Altogether, α and β parameters were predicted of 88 DES comprising hydrophilic and hydrophobic type. The available experimental data set of 7 hydrophilic and 21 hydrophobic DESs was used to construct 8 H-bond acidity and 8 H-bond basicity models. The constructed models predicted α and β values with deviation less than 2.25 and 3.14%, respectively. Therefore, these models were used for the extended scale of prediction of 19 hydrophilic and 41 hydrophobic DESs comprising choline, tetraalkylammonium, DL-menthol, and thymol-based DESs.

INTRODUCTION A deep eutectic solvent (DES) is rapidly emerging as a new kind of green solvent prepared from low-cost abundant resources. It is prepared by a mixture of organic salt and hydrogen bond donor (HBD) in a definitive molar ratio with the melting point lower than that of the individual components. Therefore, the formation of a stable DES depends on the strength of the HBD and hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA). Often, the organic salt contains a cation and an anion, where the cation acts as an additional HBD. However, a natural compound such as menthol or thymol can form a DES with carboxylic acid. Here, menthol or thymol acts as a HBA and carboxylic acid acts as a HBD. By varying the molar ratio of the components, combining different organic salts with HBD, or mixing natural compounds and carboxylic acids, a large number of DESs has been proposed in the literature. 1,2 Therefore, the physiochemical properties of DESs can be tuned depending on the molar compositions of the respective components.3 The tunable properties open up the feasibility of application of DES as a solvent in phase equilibria, 4 catalysis, 5 and chemical synthesis. 6 The combination of HBA and HBD gives DES the ability to accept and donate protons during solvation and thus form a hydrogen bond with the solute. This enhances the dissolution capability of DES, due to which it is widely used as a solvent in separation and purification processes. 7,8 One of the important properties of a solvent is polarity. Polarity defines the possible interactions between a solute and a solvent. Additionally, the polarity of a solvent influences the reaction rate, mechanism, solvation ability, and product yield. ^9 The experimental measurement of polarity involves the analysis of shifting UV–vis absorbance spectra of solvatochro- mic probes. A simplistic polarity scale is a one-parameter Dimroth–Reichardt E_T(30) scale which can only provide qualitative trends. ^10 The hydrogen bond donating ability of a solvent influences the E_T(30) polarity scale, which merely measures the polarizability. Kamlet and Taft^11 have developed a multiparametric model using a set of solvatochromic probes to assess the ability of HBD (acidity) and HBA (basicity) and polarizability of the same solvent. The Kamlet–Taft equation in the form of linear solvation energy relationship is given by XYZ = (XYZ)₀ + s(π* + dδ) + aα + bβ (1) Here, XYZ correlates the energy property of solvent parameters, whereas the solvent-independent coefficients are denoted by a, b, d, and s. The correlation of energy property of solvent parameters of the reference system is denoted by (XYZ)₀. However, all the dyes are expensive. Further, the selection of dye and experimental approach influence the solvatochromic parame- ters. 12 Therefore, the continuous improvement of experimental data set coupled with the expensive experiment makes it harder to follow a definitive chart of polarity scale. As a state-of-the-art green solvent and its ever-growing application in the separation and purification processes, construction of polarity chart becomes utmost necessity. However, a handful of literature studies are available regarding the experimental measurement of K–T parameters of DESs. Six ChCl-based DESs, four menthol-based DESs, and three quaternary ammonium-based DESs are reported by Florindo et al.13 The K–T parameters of 13 ChCl-based DESs and 3 betaine-based DESs are being reported by Cai et al.14 Teles et al. further reported the α and β values of 19 quaternary ammonium salt-based DESs.15 The K–T parameters of two quaternary ammonium salt-based DESs and one betaine-based DES are reported by Dietz et al.16 However, like other solvents, the reported data of solvatochromic parameters may vary upon the change of dye.15 The HBD and HBA present in the DES make distinctive interactions with the solute. Further, the inherent H-bond interaction between the HBA and HBD increases the complexity of nonbonded interactions with the solute. Because of the large number of DES, it will be an expensive endeavor for the experimental measurement of solvatochromic parameters of every DES. Therefore, a priori modeling of solvatochromic parameters and construction of polarity scale would ensure benchmark database for the future applications of DESs. However, to date, there is no modeling approach for the solvatochromic parameters of DESs. Hence, a modeling technique with a similar class of compounds having analogous physiochemical behavior and applications would create a benchmark step for future development. The combinatorial nature of construction, tunable nature in physiochemical properties, and their similar applications bring DESs in close analogy with ionic liquids (ILs). Therefore, to construct a predictive polarity chart of DES, we can highlight some of the modeling approaches of the solvatochromic parameters reported for ILs. To establish a well-defined, consistent, and predictive approach of solvatochromic parameters, several modeling approaches have been attempted in the literature for the case of ILs. Mente and Maroncelli performed the Monte Carlo (MC) simulation of solvent interactions in the E_T(30) scale of solvent polarity. 17 Znamenskiy and Kobrak explored the polarity of ILs using a solvatochromic dye by molecular dynamics (MD) simula- tion. 18 However, both the methods are computationally expensive. Contreras et al. proposed an empirical energy density model based on the Lewis molecular acidity of ILs. 19 Niedermeyer et al. proposed time-dependent density func- tional theory (TD-DFT) calculation involving the interaction between solvents and K-T dyes for the prediction of K-T parameters. 20 Recently, Cláudio et al. 21 and Kurnia et al. 22 predicted β and α values using the quantum chemical (QC)- based conductor-like screening model-real solvent (COSMO- RS) approach. The unimolecular QC calculation of cation and anion and subsequent correlation with the β and α values shall open up a computationally inexpensive rapid screening of solvents. In this context, we have developed a QC-based predictive approach for the hydrogen bond (H-bond) acidity (α) and hydrogen bond basicity (β) of DESs. First-principle-based predictive model COSMO-RS has been used to predict the various nonbonded interactions of DESs. The predicted nonbonded interactions are then correlated with the experimentally measured values of α and β. The correlation coefficients are later employed to develop an extended scale of predictive models. ## 2. COMPUTATIONAL METHOD ### 2.1. COSMO-RS Theory. COSMO-RS is a QC-based predictive model, where various thermodynamic properties are calculated depending on the structure of molecules. Here, molecules are assumed to be submerged in an ideal virtual conductor environment. The interactions are thereby calculated at the interface of the molecules and conductor, considering the counter-polarization and electrostatic screening. Thereafter, the molecules are considered as a collection of surface segments, and the screening charge of each segment is computed. The screening charge density, position, and area of each segment of the surface are stored in a file named "COSMO" file (.cosmo extension). Later, the pairwise interactions between the two segments are computed with a set of statistical mechanical calculations given in the literature.23,24 Misfit energy originates from the nonideal contact of two segments. van der Waals' energy is a summation of dispersion energy and cavity formation energy. The cavity formation energy arises because of the formation of a cavity inside the conductor medium to accept a molecule from the gas phase to the conductor medium. The inhomogeneous charges on the molecular surface are adequately represented by the dispersion energy. Hydrogen bond (H-bond) plays a crucial role in the formation of DES. Therefore, we have used the modified version of COSMO-RS to adequately represent the H-bond interaction in the predictive modeling.25 The screening charge densities of surface segments are standardized to accommodate into equally spaced 71 discrete bins from -0.035 to +0.035 e/Å² (an increment of 0.001 e/ Å²). Therefore, a normalized histogram of segmental areas is plotted within the limits of bins, better known as sigma profile (σ-profile). The σ-profile is the characteristic distribution of charge densities and is unique for every molecule. However, modified COSMO-RS theory segregates the hydrogen bonding segments using a Gaussian-type probability in the original σ- profile. The same is not added with the nonhydrogen bonding segmental areas. The segregation results in the representation of two σ-profiles, that is, the hydrogen bonding σ-profile and the nonhydrogen bonding σ-profile. Considering the possible attraction among the atomic pairs, the dispersion energy term is calculated by the first-order mean field term. Further, the cavity formation energy is calculated from the thermodynamics perturbation theory. The description of each energetic term and the corresponding COSMO parameters are adapted from the literature. 25,26 ## 2.2. COSMO File Generation. A two-step approach has been considered for the generation of COSMO file. In the first step, the geometries of cations, anions, and HBDs are drawn using the GaussView 5.0²⁷ visualization package. The geometries of the isolated species are optimized using the Gaussian 09 QC package using DFT.²⁸ Becke's three- 11330 https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acs.iecr.0c00574 Ind. Eng. Chem. Res. 2020, 59, 11329–11339 Industrial & Engineering Chemistry Research pubs.acs.org/IECR Article parameter-based exact exchange functional coupled with the gradient correlation of Lee, Young, and Parr, better known as the B3LYP level of theory, is employed to optimize the geometry in accordance with the 6-311+G(d) basis set. 29,30 In the COSMO calculation step, the BVP86 basis set is used to further optimize the geometries. 31 The later optimization is carried out in combination with the density fitting basis sets DGA1 and SVP32,33 to improve the relative energies and molecular structure. The newly generated COSMO file (.cosmo extension) is used in our in-house reimplementation of COSMO code to predict the respective interaction energies. 34 **2.3. The geometries of the HBAs and HBDs are independently optimized by QC calculation, followed by the generation of COSMO file. After the generation of COSMO file, the in-house reimplementation of COSMO-RS calculation gives three specific interaction energies, namely, hydrogen bonding energy ($E_{\text{HB}}$), misfit energy ($E_{\text{MF}}$), and van der Waals energy ($E_{\text{vDW}}$).$^{34}$ Therefore, a priori predictive models of H-bond acidity and basicity are linearly correlated with the three specific interactions. The linearized forms are given as α = Aα (E_HB / Σ_n E_HB) + Bα (E_MF / Σ_n E_MF) + Cα (E_VDW / Σ_n E_VDW) + Dα (2) β = Aβ (E_HB / Σ_n E_HB) + Bβ (E_MF / Σ_n E_MF) + Cβ (E_vdw / Σ_n E_vdw) + Dβ (3) Here, Aα, Bα, Cα and Dα and Aβ, Bβ, Cβ, and Dβ are two sets of coefficients used in eqs 2 and 3, respectively. However, the order of each of the interaction energies is different. Hence, to accommodate the importance of all the three energies, the calculated energies are normalized over their respective subclasses. The classification of subclasses of DESs will be discussed in detail in Section 3.2. Therefore, the coefficients of eqs 2 and 3 are calculated by fitting the interaction energies of a particular subclass of DES with the experimental values of K–T parameters. However, to calculate the coefficients of a particular subclass of DES, all known experimental K–T parameters of that subclass are considered. Computed coefficients are then used to predict the α and β values of individual compounds across the subclass. For the extended scale prediction, the corresponding coefficients of subclasses are taken along with the respective energies of that compound to predict the α and β values. By this way, the K–T parameters of the new DES are determined, whose experimental values are not available. The deviation of the predicted K–T parameters with the experimental values are determined by rmsd (%) and is given by rmsd = 100 × \left[\sum_{i=1}^{m} \frac{([K-T]_{i}^{\text{pred}} - [K-T]_{i}^{\text{expt}})^{2}}{m}\right]^{1/2} (4) Here, [K–T] defines the α or β parameter, "pred" defines the model-predicted values, "expt" defines the experimental values, and m represents the total number of DESs in a subclass. However, the absolute deviation is given by absolute deviation (%) = 100 × |[K – T]ᵢᵖʳᵉᵈ – [K – T]ᵢᵉˣᵖᵗ| (5) ## 3. The hydrophobic class is further subdivided to 34 tetraalkylammonium salt-based DESs (including chloride and bromide anions), 11 menthol-based DESs, and 17 thymol-based DESs. The magnitude of predicted energies can vary with the variation of COSMO-RS model parameters, that is, (aeff, Chb). With the variation in predicted energies, the magnitude of predicted K-T parameters will also vary. Therefore, we have used three sets of {aeff, Chb} (given in Table S7 of the Supporting Information), and subsequently, three sets of H-bond basicity of ChCl-based DESs are predicted. Suitable Methodologies of Prediction of K–T Parameters and Future Scope of Development. In the previous section, predictive approaches such as MD–MC simulation, QC calculations, and COSMO-RS framework are discussed with respect to the possible modeling pathways of K–T parameters. In the MD and MC approaches, the K–T parameters were predicted with respect to the interactions with the solvatochromic dye. However, force fields of ILs as well as DES are not reliably developed. Therefore, the accuracy of the predicted data set always remains questionable when adopting the MD approach. However, both the approaches are computationally expensive, and considering the ever-growing number of DES, the construction of such database with these approaches will take a long time. Therefore, these approaches are not suitable for a priori prediction. On the other hand, the QC-based calculation of the DES–dye complex will be relatively faster. However, generalized models based on the electronic structure calculation will likely accumulate large error in the database. This work is also derived from the optimized geometry from the electronic structure calculation coupled with the COSMO-RS formulation. In order to reduce the large error, it has been observed from the derived data set that an individual model based on the subclasses of DES shall improve the accuracy. However, the accuracy of our prediction mainly depends on the accurate theoretical description with respect to various interaction energies in the COSMO-RS framework. Therefore, the predicted and extended scale of database can be further improved by incorporating various interaction parameters given in the literature. 35,36 The existing experimental methodology of K–T parameters involves extensive solvatochromic probe. For an ever-growing list of DES, the continuous experimentation poses serious economic challenge. Further, the experimental polarity scale depends on the set of solvatochromic dyes as well as purity of the DES. Hence, the present methodology emphasizes on the identi- fication of subclasses of DES, followed by the creation of experimental data set of small number of DES of that subclass. Next, the predictive models developed within the framework of this work can predict the extended scale of K–T parameters of other DESs in the same subclass. However, a futuristic development could be the generalized model based on the group interaction parameter. However, this depends on the accurate description of interaction energies. Based on the accurate description of interaction energies of functional moieties of DES, the interaction parameters can be listed and from that the list of generalized model can be formulated. ## 4. The available experimental data set of 7 hydrophilic and 21 hydrophobic DESs was used to construct 8 H-bond acidity and 8 H-bond basicity models. Therefore, the formation of a stable DES depends on the strength of the HBD and hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA). Often, the organic salt contains a cation and an anion, where the cation acts as an additional HBD. However, a natural compound such as menthol or thymol can form a DES with carboxylic acid. This enhances the dissolution capability of DES, due to which it is widely used as a solvent in separation and purification processes. 7,8 One of the important properties of a solvent is polarity. Polarity defines the possible interactions between a solute and a solvent. Additionally, the polarity of a solvent influences the reaction rate, mechanism, solvation ability, and product yield. ^9 The experimental measurement of polarity involves the analysis of shifting UV–vis absorbance spectra of solvatochro- mic probes. Therefore, to construct a predictive polarity chart of DES, we can highlight some of the modeling approaches of the solvatochromic parameters reported for ILs. Mente and Maroncelli performed the Monte Carlo (MC) simulation of solvent interactions in the E_T(30) scale of solvent polarity. 17 Znamenskiy and Kobrak explored the polarity of ILs using a solvatochromic dye by molecular dynamics (MD) simula- tion. 18 However, both the methods are computationally expensive. COSMO-RS is a QC-based predictive model, where various thermodynamic properties are calculated depending on the structure of molecules. Here, molecules are assumed to be submerged in an ideal virtual conductor environment. The interactions are thereby calculated at the interface of the molecules and conductor, considering the counter-polarization and electrostatic screening. Thereafter, the molecules are considered as a collection of surface segments, and the screening charge of each segment is computed. The screening charge density, position, and area of each segment of the surface are stored in a file named "COSMO" file (.cosmo extension). Later, the pairwise interactions between the two segments are computed with a set of statistical mechanical calculations given in the literature.23,24 Misfit energy originates from the nonideal contact of two segments. van der Waals' energy is a summation of dispersion energy and cavity formation energy. The cavity formation energy arises because of the formation of a cavity inside the conductor medium to accept a molecule from the gas phase to the conductor medium. The inhomogeneous charges on the molecular surface are adequately represented by the dispersion energy. Hydrogen bond (H-bond) plays a crucial role in the formation of DES. Therefore, we have used the modified version of COSMO-RS to adequately represent the H-bond interaction in the predictive modeling.25 The screening charge densities of surface segments are standardized to accommodate into equally spaced 71 discrete bins from -0.035 to +0.035 e/Å² (an increment of 0.001 e/ Å²). Therefore, a normalized histogram of segmental areas is plotted within the limits of bins, better known as sigma profile (σ-profile). The σ-profile is the characteristic distribution of charge densities and is unique for every molecule. However, modified COSMO-RS theory segregates the hydrogen bonding segments using a Gaussian-type probability in the original σ- profile. The same is not added with the nonhydrogen bonding segmental areas. The segregation results in the representation of two σ-profiles, that is, the hydrogen bonding σ-profile and the nonhydrogen bonding σ-profile. Considering the possible attraction among the atomic pairs, the dispersion energy term is calculated by the first-order mean field term. Further, the cavity formation energy is calculated from the thermodynamics perturbation theory. The description of each energetic term and the corresponding COSMO parameters are adapted from the literature. 25,26 ## 2.2. COSMO File Generation. A two-step approach has been considered for the generation of COSMO file. In the first step, the geometries of cations, anions, and HBDs are drawn using the GaussView 5.0²⁷ visualization package. The chloride anion displays a stronger cation–anion interaction over the bromide anion and therefore has greater ability to accept the proton. Therefore, the chloride-based DESs have lower proton donating ability for solvent–solute interaction. Hence, they possess lower acidity than bromide-based and tetraalkylammonium-based DESs. Suitable Methodologies of Prediction of K–T Parameters and Future Scope of Development. In the previous section, predictive approaches such as MD–MC simulation, QC calculations, and COSMO-RS framework are discussed with respect to the possible modeling pathways of K–T parameters. In the MD and MC approaches, the K–T parameters were predicted with respect to the interactions with the solvatochromic dye. However, force fields of ILs as well as DES are not reliably developed. Therefore, the accuracy of the predicted data set always remains questionable when adopting the MD approach. However, both the approaches are computationally expensive, and considering the ever-growing number of DES, the construction of such database with these approaches will take a long time. Therefore, these approaches are not suitable for a priori prediction. On the other hand, the QC-based calculation of the DES–dye complex will be relatively faster. However, generalized models based on the electronic structure calculation will likely accumulate large error in the database. This work is also derived from the optimized geometry from the electronic structure calculation coupled with the COSMO-RS formulation. In order to reduce the large error, it has been observed from the derived data set that an individual model based on the subclasses of DES shall improve the accuracy. However, the accuracy of our prediction mainly depends on the accurate theoretical description with respect to various interaction energies in the COSMO-RS framework. Therefore, the predicted and extended scale of database can be further improved by incorporating various interaction parameters given in the literature. 35,36 The existing experimental methodology of K–T parameters involves extensive solvatochromic probe. For an ever-growing list of DES, the continuous experimentation poses serious economic challenge. Further, the experimental polarity scale depends on the set of solvatochromic dyes as well as purity of the DES. Hence, the present methodology emphasizes on the identi- fication of subclasses of DES, followed by the creation of experimental data set of small number of DES of that subclass. Next, the predictive models developed within the framework of this work can predict the extended scale of K–T parameters of other DESs in the same subclass. However, a futuristic development could be the generalized model based on the group interaction parameter. However, this depends on the accurate description of interaction energies. Based on the accurate description of interaction energies of functional moieties of DES, the interaction parameters can be listed and from that the list of generalized model can be formulated. ## 4. CONCLUSIONS COSMO-RS-predicted hydrogen bonding, misfit, and van der Waals energies were calculated and correlated in a four- parameter model to predict the Kamlet-Taft H-bond acidity and H-bond basicity of DESs. Altogether, α and β parameters were predicted of 88 DES comprising hydrophilic and hydrophobic type. The available experimental data set of 7 hydrophilic and 21 hydrophobic DESs was used to construct 8 H-bond acidity and 8 H-bond basicity models. The constructed models predicted α and β values with deviation less than 2.25 and 3.14%, respectively. Therefore, these models were used for the extended scale of prediction of 19 hydrophilic and 41 hydrophobic DESs comprising choline, tetraalkylammonium, DL-menthol, and thymol-based DESs. ## ASSOCIATED CONTENT **Ⓢ Supporting Information** The Supporting Information is available free of charge at https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.iecr.0c00574.
